en: The Scripture on the Ten Things Seen in a Dream by the King of Śrāvastī;
Translator Unknown.
The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove at Śrāvastī. At that time, King Prasenajit...
While lying down to sleep at night, he saw ten things in a dream.
What are these ten things?

First, he saw three jars placed together: the two on the sides were full while the one in the center was empty; from the two full jars, boiling vapors rose and drifted back and forth, yet they did not enter the empty jar.
Second, he saw that the horse ate from its mouth and also ate from its rump.
Third, he saw small trees flowering.
Fourth, he saw small trees bearing fruit.
Fifth, he saw a man cutting a rope, while behind him a sheep was eating the rope.
Sixth, he saw a fox sitting on a fine couch, eating from a golden vessel.
Seventh, he saw a great bull returning to suckle from a small calf.
Eighth, he saw four oxen bellowing as they approached from the four directions, intending to fight; just as they were about to collide, they vanished, and their whereabouts were unknown.
Ninth, he saw a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.
Tenth, he saw a mountain stream flowing a deep crimson.
Having finished his dream, the king immediately awoke; he was struck with great terror, fearing for the loss of his kingdom and his very life.

The next day, the king immediately summoned the high ministers and great officials, as well as the Brahmins who were learned in the Way and capable of interpreting dreams; they all arrived before the king, and the king then recounted to them the ten matters of his dream from the night before, asking, "Who among you can interpret this?"
Those capable of interpreting dreams immediately said,
"We can interpret them, but we fear that when the King hears them,
he will not be pleased. The King said:

"Speak it then, as you know it. The brāhmaṇa then spoke these words to the king: "The crown prince must be killed to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King; the chief consort must be killed to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King;

the attendant servants and slaves must be killed to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King; the state white elephant must be killed to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King; the prized fine horses must be killed to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King; all bedding and the precious, excellent objects worn upon the body must all be burned and used to offer as a sacrifice to the Heavenly King—only then will this king’s person be free from harm."
When the king heard that the brahmin had interpreted the dream in this manner, he became greatly distressed and withdrew into his fasting chamber to reflect.
The king had a queen named Māllī, who went to the fasting chamber where the king was and asked:
"Why have you entered the fasting chamber in such distress? Is there some fault on my part?"
The king immediately said,
"If you do not ask, perhaps hearing it will cause you distress.
The lady then asked again:
"For what reason do you grieve?
The king replied, "There is no need to ask further; hearing of it would cause you distress."
The queen spoke again:
"I am half of the King's body; when the King encounters urgency or distress, he should inform me.
The King then explained it to her, saying:
“Last night, I dreamed of ten things. First, I saw three jars:
the two on the sides were full while the one in the center was empty; from the two full jars, boiling vapors rose and circulated back and forth, yet they did not enter the empty jar.”
Second, he saw that the horse ate from its mouth and also ate from its rump.
Third, he saw small trees blooming with flowers.
Fourth, he saw small trees bearing fruit.
Fifth, he saw a man twisting a rope, while behind him a sheep stood eating the rope.
Sixth, he saw a fox sitting on a fine couch, eating from a golden vessel.
Seventh, he saw a large ox returning to suckle from a small calf.

Eighth, he saw four oxen coming from the four directions, bellowing as they approached one another with the intent to fight; yet before they had even met, the oxen vanished and could no longer be found.
Ninth, he saw a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.
Tenth, he saw a great mountain stream flowing a deep crimson.
Upon waking from the dream, he was struck with terror; such was his dream that he feared the loss of his kingdom, the loss of his son, and the loss of the people within his realm.

The following day, I immediately summoned the high ministers, great officials, and various Brahmins capable of interpreting dreams, and related my dream to them in this manner. The Brahmins who interpreted the dream said:
"Those whom the King loves, all should be used as offerings for the sacrifice to the heavens."
"For this reason, I am sorrowful.
The lady said, "O King, do not grieve!"

When people buy gold, they rub it on a stone to see whether its color is good or bad; now that the Buddha is at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, you may go there to ask the Buddha about the meaning of your dream. If the Buddha explains it, you should follow his words.
The king immediately commanded his attendants regarding the chariots and cavalry. Once the chariots and cavalry were fully prepared, the king mounted a high-canopied carriage named Vairāṇa.

At that time, several thousand chariots and cavalrymen followed him from Śrāvastī to the path leading to the Jeta Grove, Ānanda-bhūti-ārāma, where he proceeded at a slow pace. Arriving there, he descended from the carriage and went on foot to where the Buddha was.
He prostrated himself before the Buddha, touching his head to the Buddha’s feet, and then sat down to address the Buddha, saying:
"Last night, I dreamed of ten things. The first was seeing three jars placed together;
the two on the sides were full while the one in the center was empty. Steam rose from the two full jars, flowing back and forth, yet it did not enter the empty jar."
Second, he saw that horses were eating from their mouths and also eating from their rumps.
Third, he saw small trees blooming with flowers.
Fourth, he saw small trees bearing fruit.
Fifth, he saw a man binding a rope, behind whom was a sheep that proceeded to eat the rope.
Sixth, he saw a fox sitting upon a fine couch, eating from a golden vessel.
Seventh, he saw a great bull returning to suckle from a small calf.

Eighth, he saw four oxen bellowing as they came from the four directions toward one another, intending to fight; just as they were about to collide, they had vanished, and their whereabouts were unknown.
Ninth, I saw a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.
Tenth, I saw a great mountain stream flowing with water that was intensely red.
Such were my dreams; upon waking, I was struck with terror, fearing the loss of my kingdom, the loss of my son, and the loss of the people within my realm.
The King replied,
“I pray that the Buddha will explain these ten matters for me.
The Buddha then addressed the King, saying:
"Do not fear, do not fear!
That which was dreamed has no other significance; there shall be no misfortune for Your Majesty’s person, none for the kingdom, none for the crown prince, and none for the queen."
"What the King dreamed of all pertains to the giving of future generations.
The people of those future ages will not fear the Dharma; they will all be licentious and dissolute, all greedy, never satisfied with even one wife, frequently angry, foolish, and lacking in shame."

The King saw in his dream three jars placed together: the two on the sides were full while the one in the center was empty; from the two full jars, boiling vapors rose and drifted back and forth, yet they did not enter the empty jar. This signifies that in future generations, people will fail to provide for the poor, while two wealthy relatives will instead exchange gifts only among themselves. This first matter seen by the King in his dream refers precisely to this.
"O King, do not fear! Do not fear!
Neither your kingdom, nor your person, nor your wife and children shall suffer any harm.

As for the king’s dream that he saw a horse eating from its mouth and also eating from its rump: in future generations, the high ministers shall receive their stipends from the government and yet also consume the wealth of the common people. The two things seen by the king in his dream signify nothing other than this."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
Neither your kingdom, nor your person, nor your wife and children shall suffer any harm.

As for the dream in which you saw a small tree blossom, it signifies that in future generations, people will grow white-haired on their heads before they have reached the age of thirty. These three things you saw in your dream refer precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear! Do not fear!
Neither your kingdom nor your person, nor your wife and children, shall suffer any harm.

As for the small tree that you saw in your dream bearing fruit—it signifies that in future generations, young women shall marry and carry their infants, yet remain devoid of shame. This is precisely what your dream of these four things portends."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
There shall be no misfortune for your kingdom, nor for your person, nor for your wife and children.

When the King dreamed of a man twisting a rope, with a sheep behind him eating that rope, it signifies that in future generations, men shall go abroad on business and leave their wives at home; these women shall then secretly consort with other men and dwell with them. The five things the King saw in his dream refer precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear! Do not fear!
Neither your kingdom, nor your person, nor your wife and children shall suffer any harm.

As for the king’s dream of seeing a fox sitting upon a fine couch and eating from a golden vessel: this signifies that in a future life, a person of low birth shall possess great wealth and sit in a place of honor, consuming the finest delicacies. The six things seen in the king’s dream are precisely for this reason."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
There shall be no misfortune for your kingdom, nor for your person, nor for your wife and children.

As for the king’s dream of a large cow returning to suckle her own young calf: this signifies that in future generations, mothers will act as go-betweens for their daughters, bringing other men to share a chamber with their daughters; the mother herself shall guard the door, taking the money paid for the daughter's debauchery to support herself. The seven things seen in the king’s dream refer precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
There shall be no harm to your kingdom, nor to your person, nor to your wife and children.

As for the dream in which you saw four oxen bellowing from the four directions, charging toward one another as if to fight, yet before they could join, you were unaware of the oxen's whereabouts: this signifies that in future generations, the people and ministers will not stand in awe of Heaven; they will be licentious and greedy, never satisfied with even a single wife, frequently angry, foolish, shameless, and having no fear of superiors or subordinates."

If the Rain Master does not act according to the proper seasons, the sovereign, high officials, and the people must all pray for rain. Because the Rain Master sees that the sovereign, high officials, and the people are performing such practices, he raises clouds from the four directions. The sovereign, high officials, and the people all rejoice, saying:
"Clouds have already arisen from the four directions; it shall now rain."
In an instant, the clouds dispersed on their own.

The Master of Rain was still astonished by this; he wished to cause the sovereign, high officials, and the people to revere Heaven and Earth, so that they would not be licentious or greedy, would remain faithful to a single wife, and would maintain a compassionate heart free from anger. That the King saw these eight matters in his dream was precisely for this reason.
"O King, do not fear, do not fear! Neither your kingdom nor your person, nor your wife and children, shall suffer any harm.

As for the king’s dream of a great pond whose center was turbid while its four borders were clear: this signifies that in future generations, those people within Jambudvīpa will be unfilial toward their parents and disrespectful toward their elders; they will lack reciprocity and disregard the future. However, those in the bordering nations will be filial toward their parents and respectful toward their elders, possessing a sense of reciprocity. The nine things seen in the king’s dream refer precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear! Neither your kingdom, nor your person, nor your wife and children shall suffer any harm.

As for the great pond of water appearing perfectly red that you saw in your dream: it signifies that in future generations, various kings will never grow weary of their kingdoms and will raise armies; the people will rise up with weapons to fight one another, deploying chariot troops, cavalry, and infantry. They shall slay one another with chariot troops, cavalry, and infantry, until the flowing blood is perfectly red. The ten things you saw in your dream refer precisely to this."
"O King, do not fear, do not fear!
There shall be no harm to your kingdom, nor to your person, nor to your wife and children.
These dreams are all portents of matters yet to come in future lives."
The king then knelt for a long time and said:

"Upon receiving the Buddha’s teaching, my heart was filled with joy. It is like a person holding a small vessel to receive oil; when the oil is abundant and the vessel too small, they seek a larger vessel. Having obtained the large vessel, they receive more of it, becoming peaceful and free from fear."
The king immediately prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and departed.

Returning to the palace, he bestowed great rewards upon the principal queen and confiscated the stipends of all the high officials and ministers; furthermore, he no longer placed any trust in the words of the brahmins.

The *Sūtra on King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī Dreaming Ten Things*: According to this sūtra, it is a different translation of the same original text as the "Chapter on Mahāprajāpatī’s Parinirvāṇa" in the fifty-first fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Currently, the texts of the Guo and Song editions are identical in both meaning and wording; this present edition shares the same meaning as the Song edition but differs in its phrasing. It appears not to be a single translation, yet as I do not know which is correct or incorrect, I dare not omit or select between them.
However, this manuscript of the *Dān* is detailed and exhaustive; for now, I shall preserve both versions to await the discernment of future sages.
